history.heading: Ancient trade
paragraphs: Oman, on the southeastern tip of the Arabian Peninsula, has a long history of seafaring and trade. In ancient times, the land known as Magan exported copper to Mesopotamia, and the frankincense trade from Dhofar was famous; the Land of Frankincense sites are UNESCO-listed. Oman adopted Islam in the 7th century, and most Omanis follow Ibadi Islam, a distinct branch.

history.heading: Maritime empire
paragraphs: Portugal occupied Muscat and coastal towns in the 16th century, but Omanis expelled them in 1650 and built a maritime empire. Under the Al Said dynasty, founded in 1744, Oman controlled Zanzibar and parts of the East African coast and the Persian coast. Zanzibar separated in 1861.
In the 20th century Oman was isolated under Sultan Said bin Taimur. A rebellion in Dhofar lasted from 1965 to 1975.

history.heading: Modern Oman
paragraphs: In 1970 Sultan Qaboos bin Said overthrew his father and launched a rapid modernisation programme using oil revenues, building roads, schools and hospitals. He ruled for nearly 50 years. Haitham bin Tariq succeeded him in 2020.

culture.heading: Traditions
paragraphs: Arabic is the official language, and English is widely used; Baluchi, Swahili and other languages are also spoken. Omani culture emphasises hospitality, with coffee (kahwa) and dates offered to guests. Traditional dress includes the dishdasha and the khanjar dagger, a national symbol.

Oman is known for its forts, such as Bahla (UNESCO-listed), its aflaj irrigation systems, and dramatic landscapes of mountains, wadis and deserts. Shuwa, slow-cooked marinated meat, is a festive dish.

politics.heading: Absolute monarchy
paragraphs: Oman is an absolute monarchy in which the sultan holds supreme authority. The Council of Oman includes an elected consultative assembly and an appointed state council. Political parties are not permitted.
Oman has a neutral foreign policy and is known as a mediator, including between the United States and Iran.

economy.heading: Diversifying from oil
paragraphs: Oil and gas provide most government revenue, but Oman has smaller reserves than its Gulf neighbours. Its Vision 2040 plan aims to diversify through tourism, logistics (ports such as Duqm and Sohar), fisheries, mining and green hydrogen. The government introduced VAT and plans a personal income tax for high earners from 2028. The Omani rial is pegged to the US dollar.
